![Twelve biophysical sub-regions and 1.438 catalogued Palaeolithic and Mesolithic sites across Europe from 10000BC to 6000BC.](figures/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_regional_map.png)



# Abstract

Between the end of the Younger Dryas cold reversal in 10000BC and the arrival of farming communities along the Aegean and Lower Danubian frontier in 6000BC, the human population of Europe outside the eastern steppes more than tripled. Across 12 biophysical sub-regions spanning 7.148.884 km² — of which 5.072.076 km² lay outside the glaciated Greenland and High Arctic zone — aggregate population grew from 338,5k (338.500) in 10000BC to 576k (576.000) in 8000BC and reached 1,07M (1.067.500) by 6000BC [@BocquetAppel2005; @Tallavaara2015; @Zimmermann2009]. At the opening of the Holocene, more than half of Europe's foragers remained concentrated in the southern glacial refugia of Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy, where Late Magdalenian, Azilian and Epigravettian groups sustained densities of 0,1 to 0,14 inhabitants per km² [@MaierZimmermann2017; @Shao2025Pathways]. Rapid Preboreal and Boreal warming opened the northern plains, the British-Irish shelf and the deglaciating Fennoscandian Shield, lifting overall density across inhabited Europe from 0,067 inhabitants per km² in 10000BC to 0,21 inhabitants per km² in 6000BC while eustatic sea-level rise drowned Doggerland and separated Britain from the continent [@Tallavaara2015; @Kelm2023Retold]. By 6000BC, the highest regional densities belonged to two distinct environments: the estuarine wetlands of the Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries at 0,4 inhabitants per km² and the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean corridor at 0,39 inhabitants per km², where early cereal agriculture had already overtaken Iberian foraging numbers to reach 195k inhabitants [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013; @Timpson2014]. This study calibrates regional headcounts across all 12 sub-regions against radiocarbon summed probability distributions, ecological carrying capacities and a gazetteer of 1.438 catalogued habitation locales led by 1.415 radiocarbon-dated European archaeological sites.

# Background

## Glacial Refugia and the Late Pleistocene Demographic Floor

Modern human settlement in Europe during the Late Pleistocene was governed directly by ice-sheet geometry, permafrost margins and the seasonal carrying capacity of mammoth-steppe tundra [@BocquetAppel2005; @Tallavaara2015]. Long before the Holocene opened, anatomical and behavioural turnover during the Middle to Upper Palaeolithic transition had replaced sparse Neanderthal bands with Aurignacian and Gravettian hunter-gatherers organised into wider regional mating and exchange networks [@Villa2014Neandertal; @Gabora2013Contextual; @Bicho2017Early; @Schmidt2019Population]. Even at the Gravettian height around 27000BC, western and central Europe north of the Alps probably held no more than a few thousand people dispersed along loess corridors and river valleys [@MaierZimmermann2017; @Nett2021Early].

When the Last Glacial Maximum peaked between 24000BC and 18000BC, the Fennoscandian ice cap covered Scandinavia, the Baltic basin, Scotland and northern England, while Alpine glaciers sealed off the central mountain passes. Continuous permafrost extended across southern Britain, the Low Countries, northern France and the North European Plain down to the 46th parallel [@Tallavaara2015]. Human settlement north of the Loire and the Middle Danube effectively collapsed, driving surviving bands southward into three primary Mediterranean-Atlantic refugia: the Iberian-Cantabrian littoral and southwestern France (Franco-Cantabria), the Italian peninsula with its expanded Adriatic plain and the Balkan-Aegean valleys bordering the Lower Danube [@BocquetAppel2005; @Shao2025Pathways; @MaierZimmermann2017].

Within these refugia, demographic survival hinged on topographic diversity. Steep elevation gradients in Cantabria, the Pyrenees, the Apennines and the Pindus allowed small mobile bands of 25 to 50 people to move seasonally between coastal marine shelves, wooded foothills and upland ibex or chamois pastures without crossing sterile ice-margin deserts [@Shao2025Pathways; @Domingo2023Nuevo]. Yet even inside the richest shelters of Périgord and Asturias, population remained thin. Local band extinctions were frequent whenever harsh winters interrupted migratory herd routes, forcing surviving groups to rely on long-distance kin ties to replenish demographic shortfalls [@Premo2010Modeling; @Blythe2006Propagation].

## Late Glacial Recolonisation: Magdalenian, Azilian and Federmesser Expansion

Retreat of the continental ice sheets after 16000BC initiated the first sustained northward recolonisation of Europe. From the Franco-Cantabrian core, Late Magdalenian reindeer hunters moved up the Loire and Seine into the Paris Basin, crossed the Ardennes into the Meuse valley — where stratified cave sequences such as Scladina document long-term Pleistocene occupation cycles — and advanced into the Upper Rhine, Swabian Jura and Moravia [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Tallavaara2015; @BocquetAppel2005]. During the Bølling-Allerød interstadial (12700BC to 10900BC), mean July temperatures rose sharply across western Europe, drawing pioneer Creswellian and Federmesser groups across the dry English Channel river valley into southern Britain and eastward onto the sandy outwash plains of the Elbe and Oder.

That expansion suffered an abrupt climatic reverse during the Younger Dryas stadial (10900BC to 9600BC). Within a few decades, North Atlantic cooling restored tundra conditions from Ireland to Poland, pushing treeline boundaries southward and thinning northern horse and red deer herds. Specialised open-country hunters of the Ahrensburgian and Swiderian traditions tracked migratory reindeer across the North European Plain, while southern groups in Iberia, Aquitaine and Italy adapted under Azilian and Late Epigravettian lithic industries [@Tallavaara2015; @Domingo2023Nuevo].

Our earliest benchmark of 10000BC sits near the closing centuries of the Younger Dryas, just before the abrupt Preboreal warming of 9600BC. At that moment Europe's human geography still mirrored the ice-age map. Out of an estimated 338,5k inhabitants across the study domain, 175k — more than half of the entire European total — lived in the three southern cores of Iberia (65k), Franco-Aquitaine (55k) and Italy (55k). Another 48k inhabited the Balkan-Aegean zone. North of the 50th parallel, the British-Irish shelf held roughly 12k people, the vast North European Plain held 28k and newly ice-free southern Scandinavia supported barely 8k pioneer coastal hunters.

## Post-Glacial Sea-Level Rise and the Submergence of Doggerland

The warming that began around 9600BC transformed both the ecology and the coastline of Europe. As the Laurentide and Fennoscandian ice sheets melted, global sea level climbed rapidly from roughly 60 m below modern datum at 10000BC to within 10 m of present levels by 6000BC. Across northwestern and southern Europe, vast low-lying plains that had supported prime riverine foraging habitats vanished beneath the sea.

Nowhere was this territorial loss more consequential than in the southern North Sea basin. At 10000BC and 8000BC, Doggerland formed an undulating landscape of chalk hills, braided estuaries, freshwater meres and reed marshes linking eastern England directly to Denmark and the Netherlands. Early Mesolithic hunter-gatherers walked unimpeded from Yorkshire to Jutland, exploiting pike, waterfowl, elk and red deer across wetlands far richer than the drier upland heaths that survived later inundation [@Kelm2023Retold; @Tallavaara2015]. Similar lowland losses occurred in the northern Adriatic, where rising seas flooded the Great Adriatic Plain south of the Po delta, and across the Aegean Sea, where land bridges fractured into the Cycladic islands.

Between 7500BC and 6200BC, encroaching tides severed the chalk ridge of the Strait of Dover and turned Dogger Bank into a shrinking low island. Around 6200BC, two rapid shocks coincided: the final drainage of glacial Lake Agassiz triggered a century-long cold spell across the North Atlantic, and the Storegga submarine landslide off western Norway drove tsunami waves across the low-lying remnants of Doggerland, the Scottish coast and the Norwegian littoral. Britain became an island, Ireland had already been isolated for millennia and displaced coastal bands compressed into the estuaries of the Rhine, Meuse, Scheldt, Thames and Danish fjords. That compression helps explain why the Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries sub-region achieved the highest population density in Europe by 6000BC (0,4 inhabitants per km²), despite its modest modern terrestrial footprint of 156.544 km².

## Boreal Forest Closure, Aquatic Intensification and the Aegean Neolithic Threshold

As warming progressed through the Preboreal (9600BC to 8500BC) and Boreal (8500BC to 6800BC) chronozones, open birch-pine parkland gave way to dense temperate woodlands dominated by hazel, oak, elm, lime and alder. For hunters accustomed to stalking open-steppe herds, forest closure posed an ecological challenge: terrestrial ungulate biomass became more dispersed and harder to intercept, shifting subsistence from migratory reindeer to solitary woodland mammals such as red deer, roe deer, aurochs and wild boar [@Tallavaara2015; @Zimmermann2009].

Mesolithic communities answered forest closure with technological miniaturisation and aquatic intensification. Composite microlithic arrows, dug-out canoes, woven fish traps, barbed bone harpoons and domestic dogs enabled bands to harvest high-yield coastal, lacustrine and riverine niches [@Kelm2023Retold]. In Atlantic Iberia, Late Mesolithic groups established large seasonal shell-midden aggregations along the Tagus, Sado and Cantabrian estuaries — exemplified in our catalogue by Arapouco, Kobeaga II and Pendueles — while interior Spanish rock shelters such as Abrigo de Artusia, Balma Guilanya and Abrigo de los Grajos tracked upland wild game and hazel groves [@Domingo2023Nuevo]. Along the Danube Iron Gates gorge, communities at Lepenski Vir, Ajmana and Padina built trapezoidal semi-subterranean dwellings overlooking sturgeon-rich rapids, achieving near-sedentary village scale without domesticated cereals.

Across western and central Europe, ancient DNA confirms that these Mesolithic populations belonged largely to a genetically cohesive Western Hunter-Gatherer (WHG) metapopulation, exemplified by the skeleton from Abri Loschbour in Luxembourg (c. 6000BC), which remained distinct from Eastern and Scandinavian hunter-gatherers until the arrival of Anatolian-derived farmers [@Haak2015; @Olalde2018]. Along the northeastern forest fringe and eastern Baltic, Late Mesolithic foragers even began adopting early hunter-gatherer pottery traditions diffusing westward across Eurasia well before agriculture reached the boreal zone [@Pavlu2019Earliest].

In southeastern Europe, however, the demographic regime changed fundamentally before our closing horizon of 6000BC. Farming groups carrying domesticated einkorn, emmer wheat, barley, sheep, goats and cattle crossed from western Anatolia into the Aegean basin around 6800BC to 6500BC, establishing permanent mudbrick tell settlements across Thessaly, northern Greece and Macedonia — represented in our site register by Amzabegovo (Anzabegovo) and coastal caves such as Schisto [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013]. Because cereal cultivation and stock-raising could support five to ten times more people per square kilometre than broad-spectrum foraging, the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean sub-region surged from 80k inhabitants in 8000BC to 195k in 6000BC, vaulting ahead of Iberia and Italy to become Europe's largest demographic concentration right at the close of the Mesolithic era [@Pinhasi2005; @Timpson2014].

# Methodology

## Biophysical Partition of the Twelve Sub-Regions

To track demographic redistribution across sharp climatic, glacial and coastal gradients without forcing prehistoric populations into anachronistic modern state borders, MAGNETIC partitions Europe and the North Atlantic into 12 biophysical sub-regions totalling 7.148.884,3 km². Because Greenland and the High Arctic account for 2.076.808,1 km² of glaciated and polar terrain that remained entirely uninhabited prior to Palaeo-Eskimo arrival around 2500BC, all demographic density comparisons distinguish between the full continental-arctic domain (7,15M km²) and the inhabited European landmass (5.072.076,2 km²).

The 12 territorial divisions group coherent river basins, mountain watersheds and marine shelves:

1. Southern Mediterranean-Atlantic refugia: Iberian-Cantabrian Refugium (652.463,9 km²), Italian Peninsula and Po Basin (491.068,8 km²) and Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean (496.909,3 km²).
2. Temperate western basins and shelves: Franco-Aquitaine and Loire Basins (394.224,8 km²), Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries (156.544 km²) and British-Irish Insular Shelf (259.276,7 km²).
3. Central European watersheds and lowlands: Alpine and Upper Danube-Rhine (194.096,8 km²), Carpathian and Middle Danube Basin (330.528,4 km²) and North European Plain from the Elbe through the Oder and Vistula (785.578,4 km²).
4. Boreal and Arctic frontiers: Fennoscandian Shield and Baltic (1.208.169,9 km²), North Atlantic Boreal Margins covering outer western-northern Norway and adjacent boreal coasts (103.215,2 km²) and Greenland and High Arctic (2.076.808,1 km²).

This regional architecture aligns directly with palaeoclimatic pollen zones and radiocarbon clusters, allowing separate tracking of LGM refugial persistence, northern deglaciation lags and the 6000BC southeastern agrarian frontier [@Tallavaara2015; @Pinhasi2005].

## Radiocarbon Calibration and Carrying-Capacity Estimation

Prehistoric hunter-gatherers left no tax rolls, hearth counts or administrative censuses. Regional population totals $P_r(t)$ at the three benchmark years $t \in \{-10000, -8000, -6000\}$ are therefore reconstructed by triangulating three independent lines of evidence: calibrated radiocarbon summed probability distributions (SPDs), archaeological site-catchment density models and ecological carrying-capacity bounds [@BocquetAppel2005; @Zimmermann2009; @Timpson2014; @Shennan2013].

For each sub-region $r$ of terrestrial area $A_r$, regional population is expressed through its effective ecological density $d_r(t)$:

$$P_r(t) = A_r \cdot d_r(t)$$

where $d_r(t)$ is constrained between observed ethnographic and archaeological limits for temperate-to-boreal hunter-gatherers (0,005 to 0,4 inhabitants per km² prior to cereal farming) and modulated longitudinally by regional radiocarbon intensity [@BocquetAppel2005; @Zimmermann2009; @Schmidt2019Population]. Specifically, if $S_r(t)$ denotes the bias-corrected radiocarbon activity index for sub-region $r$ within a 500-year window centred on benchmark $t$, the inter-benchmark growth ratio satisfies:

$$\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)} = \left(\frac{S_r(t_2)}{S_r(t_1)}\right)^{\beta_r} \cdot \phi_r(t_1, t_2)$$

where $\beta_r \in [0,6, 0,85]$ dampens raw radiocarbon surge bias caused by taphonomic preservation decay and modern excavation clustering, and $\phi_r(t_1, t_2)$ incorporates palaeoenvironmental habitat expansion (ice-sheet retreat in Fennoscandia and the British-Irish shelf) or coastal contraction (Doggerland drowning) [@Tallavaara2015; @Timpson2014]. Compound annual growth rates between benchmarks follow standard geometric compounding:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Because hunter-gatherer populations operate near local carrying capacity with frequent stochastic band extinctions and re-fusions, long-run prehistoric growth rates stay extraordinarily low — typically 0,02% to 0,04% per annum, corresponding to doubling times of 1.800 to 3.500 years [@Premo2010Modeling; @Blythe2006Propagation]. Any departure above 0,045% per annum requires a clear ecological driver: either colonisation of newly deglaciated virgin territory (as in Fennoscandia and Scotland) or the introduction of domesticates (as in the 6000BC Aegean and Lower Danube) [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013].

## Site Gazetteer Assembly and Provenance Architecture

Alongside macro-regional population totals, MAGNETIC compiles a spatially referenced gazetteer of 2.045 catalogued habitation locales distributed across 40 modern national territories. Primary archaeological ingestion (Wave 1) assembled 1.415 radiocarbon-dated European cave, rock-shelter, shell-midden and open-air camp sites from the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus, representing 98,4% of the gazetteer. Spatial deduplication against 2.171 initial candidate records eliminated 733 redundant trench names, sub-stratigraphic duplicates and overlapping coordinates within narrow local buffers.

In addition, Wave 4 regional continuity sweeps retained 23 geographical anchor points across the North Atlantic and Greenland (12 in Greenland drawn from national statistical and GeoNames gazetteers, 10 in the Faroe Islands and 1 in Iceland from Buringh's European urban baseline), yielding an overall crowd-sourced gazetteer share of just 0,83%. Those 23 nodes serve strictly as cross-chapter geographic continuity markers for the multi-millennium MAGNETIC pipeline; Greenland's prehistoric regional headcount remains strictly zero across 10000BC, 8000BC and 6000BC, and the North Atlantic Boreal Margins population (1,5k to 8,5k) reflects maritime foraging along ice-free outer Norwegian and northern Scottish fjords rather than pre-Norse occupation of Iceland or the Faroes.

Because prehistoric sites lack historical headcount records, individual radiocarbon locales are assigned to discrete ethnographic band and macro-band carrying-capacity tiers rather than continuous urban sizes: 120 inhabitants for Late Palaeolithic open-air or cave camps active at 10000BC, 138 to 156 inhabitants for standard Early-to-Late Mesolithic seasonal base camps and 368 to 416 inhabitants for major multi-phase rock shelters, estuarine shell-midden complexes and seasonal macro-band aggregation centres active in 8000BC and 6000BC [@Schmidt2019Population; @Zimmermann2009].

# Validation

## Cross-Checks Against Palaeodemographic Benchmarks

To verify that regional estimates remain tightly bounded within established palaeodemographic consensus, MAGNETIC continental totals and densities were cross-checked against four independent archaeological syntheses. For the Late Upper Palaeolithic (Magdalenian, c. 14000BC to 11000BC), Bocquet-Appel and colleagues estimated a European meta-population of roughly 29k to 40k across core western and central archaeologically surveyed regions, scaling upward substantially once southern Mediterranean refugia, the Balkans and coastal plains are fully included [@BocquetAppel2005]. Using bioclimatic envelope modelling across the entire European continent, Tallavaara and colleagues reconstructed a Last Glacial Maximum low of approximately 130k people around 21000BC, expanding sharply to roughly 330k to 410k during the Late Glacial warming before the Holocene threshold [@Tallavaara2015].

Our 10000BC domain figure of 338,5k aligns closely with the central corridor of those bioclimatic reconstructions. Equally important, the implied mean density across inhabited Europe in 10000BC — 0,067 inhabitants per km² — matches the archaeological density envelope derived by Schmidt and Zimmermann for Upper Palaeolithic core catchments (0,01 to 0,15 inhabitants per km² depending on regional productivity) [@Schmidt2019Population; @MaierZimmermann2017].

By 6000BC, inhabited European density reaches 0,21 inhabitants per km², with temperate river basins clustering between 0,23 and 0,4 inhabitants per km². That range agrees directly with Zimmermann, Hilpert and Wendt's comparative synthesis of pre-Neolithic European forager densities, which places richest Late Mesolithic estuarine and lacustrine landscapes near 0,2 to 0,5 inhabitants per km² while interior woodlands remain near 0,1 to 0,2 inhabitants per km² — roughly an order of magnitude below mature Linearbandkeramik (LBK) farming densities (0,6 to 2 inhabitants per km²) that emerged after 5500BC [@Zimmermann2009; @Shennan2013].

Across the four millennia from 10000BC to 6000BC, the overall continental growth rate averaged 0,029% per annum (0,027% from 10000BC to 8000BC and 0,031% from 8000BC to 6000BC). The three old southern refugia grew at the slowest proportional rates — 2,31x in Iberia, 2,45x in Franco-Aquitaine and 2,64x in Italy — because they started closer to their Late Glacial carrying capacity. By contrast, newly deglaciated northern zones expanded far faster from near-zero baselines: 6,5x in Fennoscandia and the Baltic, 5,67x along the North Atlantic Boreal Margins and 4,58x across the British-Irish shelf. Only one southern sub-region matched northern proportional growth: the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean grew 4,06x (more than doubling in the second two-millennium interval alone, from 80k to 195k), capturing the unmistakable demographic signature of the Early Neolithic expansion [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013].

# Results

## Continental Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 6000BC)

Europe's prehistoric demographic curve from 10000BC to 6000BC exhibits steady, accelerating post-glacial expansion rather than stagnation (Figure \ref{fig:palaeo-trajectory}). Between 10000BC and 8000BC, aggregate population rose by 237,5k (+70,16%) to reach 576k. Between 8000BC and 6000BC, it added a further 491,5k (+85,33%) to reach 1.067.500 inhabitants — passing the one-million mark for the first time in European prehistory.

<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_magnetic/1.0-prehistoric-palaeolithic-mesolithic-europe/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:palaeo-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Aggregate demographic trajectory for Europe and its four largest sub-regions from 10000BC to 6000BC (Panel A) and sub-regional population density rankings in 6000BC (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

More revealing than the headline total is the internal redistribution of Europe's population. In 10000BC, the three Western Mediterranean and Atlantic refugia (Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy) accounted for 51,7% of all European inhabitants, while temperate central and northern Europe (Britain, Low Countries, Alpine-Upper Danube, North European Plain, Fennoscandia and North Atlantic margins) held only 26,4%. By 8000BC, the refugial share had slipped to 45,5% as Boreal woodlands and North Sea lowlands filled in. By 6000BC, the traditional western refugia represented just 40,3% of Europe's population, whereas temperate central-northern Europe accounted for 32,5% and the Danubian-Balkan-Aegean axis surged to 27,2% (18,3% in the Balkan-Aegean alone plus 8,9% in the Carpathian-Middle Danube basin). Europe was no longer a cluster of isolated southern pockets; it had become a continuous, ecologically filled mosaic stretching from Gibraltar to the Arctic Circle.

## Southern Refugia and the Mediterranean-Atlantic Core

The Iberian-Cantabrian Refugium (652.463,9 km²) opened the Holocene as Europe's most populous region at 65k inhabitants (0,1 inhabitants per km²), expanding to 95k in 8000BC and 150k in 6000BC (0,23 inhabitants per km²). Iberia also supplies the largest regional share of our archaeological gazetteer with 242 catalogued sites (165 in Spain, 43 in Portugal, 3 in Andorra and 1 in Gibraltar). Settlement was strongly polarised between two ecological strips: the wet Atlantic-Cantabrian facade and the Mediterranean karst valleys of the Ebro and Levant, separated by the drier interior Meseta [@Shao2025Pathways; @Domingo2023Nuevo]. Along the Cantabrian coast and Pyrenees, dense multi-phase rock shelters such as Abrigo de Artusia, Abrigo de Kobeaga II, Abrigos de Pendueles, Balma Guilanya and Balma Margineda sustained recurring seasonal camps across the Azilian and Asturian transitions. Along the Atlantic estuaries of Portugal, sites such as Arapouco and Armação Nova anchored intensive Late Mesolithic shell-midden foraging that persisted even as Cardial Neolithic pioneers began sailing westward along the Mediterranean rim after 5800BC [@Bicho2017Early; @Shao2025Pathways].

Immediately across the Pyrenees, the Franco-Aquitaine and Loire Basins (394.224,8 km²) held Europe's highest regional density at the opening of the Holocene: 55k inhabitants in 10000BC (0,14 inhabitants per km²), rising to 85k in 8000BC and 135k in 6000BC (0,34 inhabitants per km²), documented across 216 catalogued sites. Inheriting the dense Magdalenian networks of the Dordogne, Vézère, Lot and Garonne valleys, Azilian and Sauveterrian foragers spread northward across the Loire and Seine catchments into wooded river valleys and sandy uplands such as Bois de Saponay. Even as northern France transitioned into closed Boreal oak-hazel forest, Aquitaine and the Brittany coast retained rich salmon rivers and marine estuaries capable of sustaining persistent Mesolithic communities.

Across the Alps, the Italian Peninsula and Po Basin (491.068,8 km²) matched Franco-Aquitaine at 55k in 10000BC (0,11 inhabitants per km²), expanding to 82k in 8000BC and 145k in 6000BC (0,3 inhabitants per km²), supported by 199 catalogued sites. Late Epigravettian groups in Sicily (including coastal locales near Aci Trezza), Liguria, Tuscany and the Alpine piedmont (such as Alba) adapted smoothly to Holocene warming, shifting upward into high Alpine summer hunting camps in the Dolomites and Trentino as snowlines retreated. Although rising Adriatic waters gradually drowned the wide glacial plain southeast of Venice, the fertile Po river terraces, Tyrrhenian lagoons and southern Apulian coasts maintained steady growth — and by 6000BC southern Italy stood on the immediate threshold of Impressed Ware maritime colonisation from across the Strait of Otranto [@Pinhasi2005].

## Balkan-Aegean Expansion and Danubian Corridors

The single greatest demographic transformation of the 10000BC to 6000BC epoch unfolded in the Balkan-Lower Danube and Aegean sub-region (496.909,3 km²). At 10000BC, its 48k inhabitants (0,097 inhabitants per km²) trailed Iberia, France and Italy, and at 8000BC its 80k inhabitants (0,16 inhabitants per km²) still ran parallel to the Italian trajectory. Between 8000BC and 6000BC, however, the region more than doubled to 195k inhabitants (0,39 inhabitants per km²), overtaking every other part of Europe.

Two distinct processes drove this surge, both visible among the sub-region's 84 catalogued sites (39 in Greece, 18 in Serbia, 10 in Bulgaria, 5 each in North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro, plus 3 in Albania and 2 in European Turkey). First, in the Iron Gates gorges of the Lower Danube, complex Mesolithic fishing communities at sites such as Ajmana, Banja and the Lepenski Vir cluster achieved semi-sedentary village density by exploiting migrating beluga sturgeon and carp along rocky river narrows. Second, and decisively, Anatolian farming populations established permanent agro-pastoral villages across the Thessalian plain, coastal Thrace and the Vardar-Morava corridor — marked in our gazetteer by early stratigraphic complexes at Amzabegovo (Anzabegovo) in North Macedonia and coastal Greek caves such as Schisto [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013]. Unlike hunter-gatherers bound by seasonal resource troughs, early farmers stored cereal grain over winter, shortened birth intervals and sustained rapid local population doubling [@BocquetAppel2005; @Timpson2014].

Upstream along the Danube, the Carpathian and Middle Danube Basin (330.528,4 km²) grew steadily from 26k in 10000BC (0,079 inhabitants per km²) to 48k in 8000BC and 95k in 6000BC (0,29 inhabitants per km²). Although modern alluvial burial across the Great Hungarian Plain restricts archaeological recovery to 32 catalogued sites (17 in Hungary, 16 in Romania across basin edges, plus Slovak and Serbian margins), Upper Palaeolithic loess sites such as Crvenka-At demonstrate deep Pleistocene continuity along the southern Carpathian rim [@Nett2021Early]. By 6000BC, Early Neolithic Körös and Starčevo farming pioneers were already pressing northward along the Tisza and Körös rivers, setting the stage for the explosive Linearbandkeramik expansion of the sixth millennium BC [@Pinhasi2005].

To the west, the Alpine and Upper Danube-Rhine sub-region (194.096,8 km²) climbed from 22k in 10000BC (0,11 inhabitants per km²) to 40k in 8000BC and 75k in 6000BC (0,39 inhabitants per km², third highest in Europe), documented across 80 catalogued sites. As valley glaciers retreated up the Rhône, Rhine, Inn and Upper Danube corridors, post-glacial lakes — Geneva, Neuchâtel, Constance and Federsee — created exceptionally productive wetland ecotones. Rock shelters along the Jura and Swiss plateau, exemplified by Abri Freymond, anchored seasonal movements between winter lakeside fisheries and summer alpine ibex valleys.

## Northwestern Shelves, the Rhine-Meuse Estuary and the North European Plain

North of the Loire and the central European uplands, the Boreal Mesolithic witnessed a remarkable filling-in of lowland river basins and maritime estuaries. The Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries sub-region (156.544 km²) experienced one of the strongest demographic consolidations in pre-agrarian Europe, expanding 3,44-fold from 18k in 10000BC (0,12 inhabitants per km²) to 35k in 8000BC and 62k in 6000BC — reaching 0,4 inhabitants per km², the highest regional density on the continent. Its 130 catalogued sites (including Abri Loschbour in Luxembourg, Achmer in Lower Saxony, Almere-Hout in the Dutch polderlands and karst shelters along the Belgian Meuse [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Olalde2018]) reflect a landscape uniquely enriched by post-glacial hydrology. As sea level rose across the southern North Sea, river gradients flattened, turning the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta into an expansive mosaic of sandy river dunes (*donken*), tidal creeks, alder carrs and reedbeds teeming with waterfowl, eel, pike, beaver and wild boar. Displaced populations retreating inland from submerged Doggerland augmented local density along this estuary rim.

Across the newly formed English Channel, the British-Irish Insular Shelf (259.276,7 km²) grew 4,58-fold from 12k in 10000BC (0,046 inhabitants per km²) to 28k in 8000BC and 55k in 6000BC (0,21 inhabitants per km²), recorded across 144 catalogued sites (plus additional English Channel/North Sea margin sites grouped on the continental border). At 10000BC, human presence was sparse and concentrated in southern English caves and open-air Federmesser camps. By 8000BC, Early Mesolithic Maglemosian-related hunters occupied lakeside base camps across Yorkshire (the Star Carr horizon), the Thames-Kennet valley, Wales and northern England (such as Bart's Shelter in Cumbria), while pioneer maritime foragers crossed the Irish Sea to colonise Ireland (Mount Sandel horizon) and western Scotland (including Auchareoch on Arran). Following final insular separation around 6200BC, Late Mesolithic Britain and Ireland evolved distinctive narrow-blade microlithic and coastal shell-midden traditions (such as Oronsay in the Hebrides) insulated from continental ceramic developments for another two millennia.

East of the Weser, the expansive North European Plain from the Elbe through the Oder and Vistula (785.578,4 km²) rose 3,39-fold from 28k in 10000BC (0,036 inhabitants per km²) to 55k in 8000BC and 95k in 6000BC (0,12 inhabitants per km²), anchored by 207 catalogued sites across northern Germany, Denmark and Poland. Despite its large absolute population — fourth equal with the Carpathian basin by 6000BC — mean density remained modest across the sandy glacial outwash soils of Brandenburg, Pomerania and Masovia. Population clustered tightly around glacial tunnel valleys, moraine lakes and Baltic coastal inlets. In eastern Denmark and Schleswig-Holstein, bog wetlands such as Aamosen and coastal stations across the western Baltic supported exceptionally rich Maglemosian and Kongemose fisheries that laid the ecological foundation for the sedentary Ertebølle shell-midden society of the fifth millennium BC [@Kelm2023Retold].

## Deglaciating Boreal Frontiers and the Uninhabited High Arctic

No part of Europe changed its physical geography faster between 10000BC and 6000BC than the Fennoscandian Shield and Baltic sub-region (1.208.169,9 km²). At 10000BC, the remnants of the Scandinavian ice sheet still blanketed central Sweden, Finland and interior Norway, confining roughly 8k pioneer hunters (0,007 inhabitants per km²) to the ice-free western Swedish archipelago, southern Scania and narrow strips of the ice-free Norwegian coast (Fosna-Hensbacka and Ahrensburgian traditions). As the ice cap collapsed rapidly during the Preboreal — disappearing entirely from the Swedish interior by 7000BC — post-glacial isostatic rebound lifted new coastal archipelagos out of the Ancylus Lake and early Littorina Sea.

Human groups tracked the retreating ice front at remarkable speed, driving a 6,5-fold expansion to 24k in 8000BC and 52k in 6000BC (0,043 inhabitants per km²), recorded across 81 catalogued sites (46 in Norway across shield and boreal margins, 34 in Sweden, 9 in Finland and 4 across the Baltic states). Pioneers moving around the ice-free Arctic coast of Norway established the Komsa complex in Finnmark before 9000BC, while groups advancing from Karelia and the southeastern Baltic populated inland Finland (Suomusjärvi culture) all the way north to sub-arctic river valleys such as Atsinki at 65,57°N. Even at 6000BC, however, boreal conifer forests imposed strict winter calorie bottlenecks, keeping inland densities below 0,05 inhabitants per km² and tying most settlements to coastal seal hunting, salmon rivers and lake outlets.

Along the exposed North Atlantic Boreal Margins (103.215,2 km²) — encompassing outer fjordic western and northern Norway and the northernmost British-Shetland boreal fringe — population expanded 5,67-fold from 1,5k in 10000BC to 4k in 8000BC and 8,5k in 6000BC (0,082 inhabitants per km²). Warm North Atlantic Drift waters kept outer Norwegian fjords ice-free year-round, supporting marine mammal and cod foraging at densities nearly double the interior Fennoscandian Shield. By contrast, Iceland and the Faroe Islands lay beyond the practical open-ocean voyaging horizon of Mesolithic skin boats, and Greenland and the High Arctic (2.076.808,1 km²) remained entirely uninhabited (0 inhabitants) throughout all three benchmarks; human colonisation of Greenland awaited the eastward spread of Arctic Small Tool (Independence I and Saqqaq) Palaeo-Eskimo hunters across the Canadian High Arctic more than three millennia later, around 2500BC.

## Pre-Urban Habitation Structure and Site Distribution

Unlike agrarian, classical or mediaeval Europe — where administrative capitals, ports and market towns produce a steep power-law rank-size curve — Palaeolithic and Mesolithic Europe possessed no urban hierarchy. Figure \ref{fig:palaeo-hierarchy} illustrates this structural reality directly across all 1.438 catalogued habitation records: rather than a Zipfian slope ($\alpha \approx -1$), the rank-size profile forms a series of flat ecological plateaus corresponding to band and macro-band carrying-capacity tiers.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:palaeo-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_magnetic/1.0-prehistoric-palaeolithic-mesolithic-europe/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:palaeo-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Top catalogued Palaeolithic and Mesolithic habitation complexes (Panel A) and stepped band-tier rank-size distribution across 1.438 sites (Panel B), 10000BC to 6000BC.</figcaption>
</figure>

Specifically, 306 major multi-phase rock shelters, estuarine shell-midden complexes and seasonal macro-band aggregation locales — led alphabetically by Abri Freymond, Abri Loschbour, Abri des Boeufs, Abrigo de Artusia, Abrigo de Kobeaga II and Achmer — sit on the upper tier of 416 inhabitants at 6000BC (up from 368 at 8000BC). Beneath that aggregation ceiling, 660 standard Late Mesolithic seasonal camps occupy the 156-person tier, 434 Early-Middle Mesolithic locales sit at 138 persons and 15 purely Late Palaeolithic camps peak at 120 persons, alongside 23 low-tier Arctic and North Atlantic spatial continuity anchors (80 to 118 persons). In demographic terms, Europe's hunter-gatherers lived in flat, horizontally linked networks of residential bands rather than hierarchical central places [@Schmidt2019Population; @Premo2010Modeling; @Rowe2019Impact].

Comparing density with site recovery intensity highlights an instructive methodological pattern: the Rhine-Meuse and Low Countries (8,3 sites per 10.000 km²), British-Irish shelf (5,55), Franco-Aquitaine (5,48), Alpine-Upper Danube (4,12), Italy (4,05) and Iberia (3,71) enjoy dense modern rescue archaeology and karst cave preservation, whereas the Carpathian basin (0,97) and Balkan-Aegean (1,69) suffer far heavier Holocene alluvial burial despite high ecological carrying capacity. Regional headcounts therefore rely on joint bioclimatic and radiocarbon scaling rather than naive raw site summation [@Tallavaara2015; @Timpson2014].

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern prehistoric demographic reconstruction across Palaeolithic and Mesolithic Europe.

First, post-glacial sea-level rise erased Europe's prime coastal foraging landscapes. Between 10000BC and 6000BC, Doggerland, the English Channel valley, the Great Adriatic Plain and substantial sections of the Atlantic and Aegean shelves disappeared beneath marine sediments. Because coastal and estuarine niches typically supported the highest hunter-gatherer densities, terrestrial site catalogues systematically under-sample early littoral populations. Regional totals partially correct for this loss through ecological carrying-capacity bounds, yet the exact headcount displaced from Doggerland into Britain and the Low Countries remains bounded within roughly $\pm 25\%$ [@Tallavaara2015; @Kelm2023Retold].

Second, archaeological visibility varies starkly by geology and modern excavation intensity. Limestone karst regions in Cantabria, Périgord, the Belgian Meuse and the Swiss Jura preserve stratified bone and charcoal in caves and rock shelters [@Vonhof2024Improving; @Domingo2023Nuevo], while waterlogged peat bogs in Denmark and the Netherlands preserve organic wood and bone tools. Conversely, acidic glacial sands on the North European Plain destroy uncharred bone, and thick Holocene river alluvium across the Po, Danube and Tisza basins buries Mesolithic living floors several metres underground [@Nett2021Early]. National survey budgets reinforce these physical differences: France (271 sites), the United Kingdom (174), Spain (165), Italy (114) and Germany (108) together account for 57,9% of the entire gazetteer.

Third, radiocarbon summed probability distributions carry known calibration and dietary biases [@Timpson2014; @Shennan2013]. Atmospheric carbon-14 plateaux during the Younger Dryas and Preboreal compress or stretch apparent site clusters, while freshwater and marine reservoir effects can skew dates on human bone from riverine or coastal fishers by 200 to 500 years unless corrected by stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes. Similarly, assigning standardised band tiers (120 to 416 persons) to excavated radiocarbon locales provides consistent spatial weighting across 1.438 sites, but individual rock shelters often housed smaller nuclear bands of 15 to 40 people over repeated seasonal visits rather than 400 permanent residents simultaneously [@Schmidt2019Population; @Zimmermann2009].

Fourth, the multi-chapter gazetteer retains 23 Wave-4 spatial anchor records across Greenland (12), the Faroe Islands (10) and Iceland (1) drawn from national statistical and municipal gazetteers to preserve cross-era node continuity across the wider MAGNETIC atlas. Those records carry zero weight in Greenland's regional demographic aggregate (0 inhabitants across all three benchmarks) and do not imply Mesolithic occupation of Iceland or the Faroes.

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 6000BC, Europe underwent its first great post-glacial demographic expansion. Driven by rapid Holocene warming, the replacement of tundra by temperate hazel-oak woodlands and the colonisation of newly deglaciated northern lands, aggregate population more than tripled from 338,5k in 10000BC to 576k in 8000BC and 1,07M (1.067.500) in 6000BC. Inhabited European density rose from 0,067 to 0,21 inhabitants per km² — approaching the upper ecological ceiling of non-agricultural foraging across temperate river valleys and marine estuaries.

That growth fundamentally rebalanced the continent's human geography. Whereas southern refugia in Iberia, Franco-Aquitaine and Italy held more than half of Europe's inhabitants at the close of the Younger Dryas, four millennia of northward movement filled the British-Irish shelf, the Rhine-Meuse delta, the North European Plain and the deglaciating Fennoscandian Shield up to the Arctic Circle. By 6000BC, however, the long equilibrium of European hunter-gatherer demography was already breaking. Along the Aegean littoral and the Lower Danube, early agro-pastoral communities had pushed Balkan population to 195k — eclipsing every western forager domain and launching the Neolithic transition that would multiply Europe's population many times over during the millennia ahead [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013; @Haak2015].

## Provenance Corpus Breakdown

Table \ref{tab:provenance-summary} documents the five source corpora contributing to the chapter's settlement register, confirming that 98,4% of catalogued locales derive directly from primary European radiocarbon archaeological inventories.
